newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - BMW unveils plans for baby Land Rover.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BMW unveils plans for baby Land Rover.

text.p: Rover Group, the British car making arm of Germany's BMW, on Tuesday unveiled massive investment plans for a major new product -- the "baby Land Rover" which will take on Japanese rivals in the British and world markets.
Rover's new chief executive, Dr Walter Hasselkus, satisfied long-standing market speculation by announcing the new investment plan at the British International Motor Show in Brimingham.

The new vehicle, dubbed by Hasselkus the "baby Land Rover" and smaller than four-wheel drive specialist Land Rover's current Range Rover and Discovery models, will take Rover into a completely new market and is part of the British group's 3.0 billion pounds ($4.75 billion) rolling investment programme.

As well as safeguarding 12,000 jobs at the Solihull Land Rover factory in central England, the new chief executive told reporters at the show that it will also inject 3.5 billion pounds of new business into the UK automotive component industry.
This in itself will support a further 10,000 jobs in that industry, with British companies supplying 87.5 percent of the baby Land Rover components.
Hasselkus refused to be drawn on which companies will benefit from the new vehicle which will go on sale in early 1998.

But the chief executive, who is the first German to take the reins at the famous British motor group, told Reuters in an interview, "We are looking for conquest sales and we are definitely shooting for significant extra volumes."
"The baby Land Rover is very much an export product," he said, adding that he hoped exports would account for 70 percent of production.
Hasselkus said that the major investment programme meant that the company was more likely to hit a break-even position, from a 158 million pounds loss last year, by 2000.
If the group had not embarked on its heavy investment plan, profitability could have been hit within two years, he said.
"We take a long-term view and want Rover's performance to be successful and meaningful. To achieve this we have to invest and that is costly," he told Reuters.
Rover expects to sell over 500,000 units this year, up from 484,000 last year.
1997 is seen remaining fairly steady, with purely generic growth, but a gain is expected in 1998 when the baby Land Rover makes its debut.

A new seven-acre factory complex is being built at Solihull which will start production of the new Land Rover models towards the end of 1997. Rover said that by 2000 its Land Rover unit production would be three times higher than the 68,000 vehicles made in 1993.

World demand for Land Rover vehicles showed continued growth, Rover said, with sales rising by more than 12 percent so far this year. Big increases had been seen in the U.S., Japan, Germany and South Africa, it said. ($1=.6317 Pound)
